# Proper critical sections: exact two-sided identities and a transverse test

This note studies an actual cap in continuous dimension two. It does not
prove that a section center is a center of the original mixed set, and it
does not assume that a stationary or minimizing cap's source is globally
deepest over that set.

## 1. Flattening the cut preserves the mixed measure

Let C be a convex body in R^n times R^2, with positive mixed area. Let
Y=(z0,x0), z0 integer, belong to a positive-area fiber, and let

    H={a.(z-z0)+u.(x-x0)>=0}, u nonzero,

be proper on every positive-area integer fiber. Choose an orthonormal
continuous basis (f,e), with e=u/|u|, and use coordinates

    z'=z-z0,
    s=f.(x-x0),
    t=e.(x-x0)+a.(z-z0)/|u|.

This is an invertible affine map fixing the integer-coordinate structure;
its restriction to each fixed integer fiber is an isometry followed by
a translation, so it preserves fiber areas and section lengths. It takes
Y to 0 and H to {t>=0}. All ambient halfspaces transform to ambient
halfspaces. In these coordinates write K_z for the two-dimensional fiber.
Let P be the finite set of positive-area integer fibers. Set

    I_z={s:(s,0) in K_z}, W=sum_(z in P) length(I_z).

Every I_z is a positive-length interval. The derivative section measure
is sum_(z in P) length on these intervals. In the unflattened coordinates
its common coarea factor is 1/|u|, which cancels in a centroid equation.

For perturbations through the same source,

    H_epsilon={t+epsilon[a'.z+b's]>=0},

proper-section differentiation by vertical intervals and dominated
convergence gives

    d/d epsilon mu(H_epsilon)|_0
       =sum_(z in P) integral_(I_z)(a'.z+b's) ds.         (1)

The differentiating plane intersects each two-dimensional fiber properly;
almost every point of its interval section is an interior point of that
fiber. The exceptional interval endpoints are length-null, so no smooth
boundary assumption is needed. Bounded fibers give a uniform bound on
the divided changes of interval lengths. Thus, if H minimizes cap mass
under normal perturbations through Y, (1) vanishes for every a',b', and

    sum |I_z| z=0,   sum integral_(I_z) s ds=0.           (2)

The source is exactly the mixed centroid of this derivative section.
No assertion about the centroid of any individual I_z follows.

### Removing unmeasured fibers before applying a section theorem

An original zero-area fiber can lie in t=0 and carry positive section
length. Such length is absent from (1), so one must not identify its
measure with the full intrinsic measure of the original cut section.
There is a direct reduction when the source lies in a positive fiber.
Restrict the integer projection of C to conv(P). Every real point of
conv(P) is a convex combination of positive-fiber bases, and its fiber
contains their weighted Minkowski combination, which has positive area.
Consequently the integer points of conv(P) are exactly P. This restriction
preserves every positive integer fiber, all mixed area, and the source,
and removes every unmeasured integer fiber.

If P has affine rank r<n, identify aff(P) with R^r using a basis of the
full lattice (aff(P)-z0) intersect Z^n. This identifies its integer points
with Z^r. Each continuous fiber remains unchanged, so both its area and
its cut length remain unchanged. Every restricted ambient halfspace is a halfspace in the reduced
coordinates, the whole reduced affine space, or the empty set; every
proper reduced halfspace conversely extends to the original space. A
containing trace cannot be empty, and a full trace cannot lower depth. The restricted body has nonempty relative interior:
combine r+1 affinely independent bases and positive-area fiber balls.
Its cut section has full relative dimension r+1, because its plane cuts
all those positive fibers properly. After this explicitly tracked
reduction, the actual induced mixed interval section has measure W and
centroid 0. This permits a legitimate lower-dimensional section theorem;
it does not transfer that theorem to original cap areas.

## 2. The exact two-sided section-to-volume decomposition

For each z in P project K_z onto its s-axis, obtaining an interval J_z.
Its vertical fibers are intervals

    f_z(s)<=t<=g_z(s), s in J_z,

with f_z convex and g_z concave on the interior and their compact-body
endpoint values understood. Define

    I_z={s:f_z(s)<=0<=g_z(s)},
    J_z^+={s:f_z(s)>0}, J_z^-={s:g_z(s)<0}.

Writing Q=mu({t>=0}) and M=mu(C intersect the mixed lattice), Fubini gives

    Q=sum_z integral_(I_z) g_z(s) ds
          +sum_z integral_(J_z^+) [g_z(s)-f_z(s)] ds,    (3)
    M-Q=sum_z integral_(I_z) [-f_z(s)] ds
          +sum_z integral_(J_z^-) [g_z(s)-f_z(s)] ds.    (4)

These include positive and negative overhangs whose vertical projections
miss the section. Tangencies affect only zero area. For every measurable
subset G of the (z,s) section coordinate space, the same identities with
all domains restricted to G give the corresponding vertically extended
cap masses. A section-depth theorem controls unweighted lengths of
I_z intersect G. Equations (3)--(4) instead involve distinct height
weights and possibly both kinds of overhang. Neither term may be removed
without a geometric argument.

Equivalently, with I_z(h)={s:(s,h) in K_z} and
W(h)=sum_z |I_z(h)|, ordinary Cavalieri gives

    mu({t>=h})=integral_h^infinity W(v) dv,
    mu({t<=h})=integral_(-infinity)^h W(v) dv.            (5)

For finite fibers these tails are absolutely continuous and have
derivative -W(h) and +W(h), respectively, at almost every h. At the
proper levels in question W is continuous, so the derivative exists.
An identity about W(0), its centroid, or its directional tails supplies
no relation between the two entire integrals in (5).

## 3. A section point cannot strictly improve an attained original cap

This simple observation does not require convexity. If H contains a
source Y and attains its raw depth Q, every Y' in S intersect H has
original depth at most Q, because H is an admissible containing halfspace
for Y'. In particular every point of S intersect boundary(H), including
any lower-dimensional section center, has original depth at most Q.
A strict improvement obtained from that section therefore must include
a transverse displacement. Section membership or improved section depth
alone cannot give it.

## 4. A convex roof family with an exact proper minimizing cap

Let D be a full-dimensional compact convex body in R^n times R,
centrally symmetric about 0, with 0 at an actual positive integer fiber.
Let g be a continuous positive concave function on D, and choose
L>=max_D g. Form the convex body

    C={ (z,s,t):(z,s) in D, -L<=t<=g(z,s) }.

Let nu be mixed length on D, W=nu(D), and Q=integral_D g dnu. Its
mixed area is

    M=LW+Q.                                             (6)

Its section at t=0 is exactly D with centroid 0, and H={t>=0} is
proper on every positive-area fiber. More strongly, H is a global
minimum among ALL closed ambient halfspaces containing Y=0, with raw
depth exactly Q. To prove the lower bound, use the actual mixed subset
induced by

    E={ (z,s,t):(z,s) in D,
                       -g(-z,-s)<=t<=g(z,s) }.

It lies in C because g<=L, is centrally symmetric about 0, and has
mixed area 2Q. Reflection preserves the lattice, fiber area, and E.
Every closed halfspace containing 0 contains at least one member of
each reflected pair, including pairs on its boundary. It therefore
contains at least Q of E's area. The cap {t>=0} has area Q exactly,
so it attains the infimum. This proof includes pure integer halfspaces
and normals coupling every coordinate.

For fixed D and g, the minimizing cap and its section do not change as
L increases, while

    depth_C(0)=Q/(LW+Q) tends to zero.                    (7)

The section can simultaneously have the maximum possible depth 1/2.
Thus even a perfectly deep, centroidal mixed section and a globally
minimizing proper cap give no positive original normalized-depth lower
bound at their source. This is NOT a global-deepest-point counterexample:
C contains the symmetric lower cylinder D times [-L,0], whose actual
center (0,0,-L/2) has raw depth at least LW/2. For L>2Q/W this already
exceeds Q. The distinction is essential.

## 5. Exact rational directional-transfer failure

Take n=1,

    D=[-1,1] times [-1,1],
    g(z,s)=5/4-s, L=3.

The complete integer base set is {-1,0,1}; all original fibers have
positive area. The section has three identical intervals [-1,1],
W=6, centroid 0, and maximum normalized section depth exactly 1/2.
Reflection gives the lower bound, and {s>=0} through 0 gives equality.
Here

    Q=15/2, M=51/2, depth_C(0)=5/17.

The vertically extended section halfspace G={s>=0} captures section
length 3, half of W. Yet the portion of the positive critical cap lying
above G has area

    3 integral_0^1(5/4-s) ds=9/4,

which is only 3/10 of Q, strictly below both 1/2 and Gamma_2=4/9.
The negative-side portion above G has area 9, exactly half of the total
negative-side area 18. Thus both sides are explicitly tracked; a perfect
half-section division can have substantially different positive-cap and
negative-cap fractions, even at an actual full-normal globally minimizing
proper cap. No oblique-halfspace restriction or stationary-only surrogate
is used in this certificate.

The ratios in (7) can be made arbitrarily small by increasing the
rational L, still retaining all proper cuts and the same section. Again,
the source is not asserted to maximize original depth over S.

## 6. A genuine transverse improvement, with its necessary growth condition

The roof model also gives a positive, exactly scoped transfer mechanism.
For a real h satisfying

    (max_D g-L)/2 <= h <= min_D g,

and g(z,s)+g(-z,-s)>=2h on D, the actual source Y_h=(0,0,h) has raw
mixed depth exactly

    Q-hW.                                               (8)

Indeed the cap {t>=h} has that area. The subset

    E_h={ (z,s,t):(z,s) in D,
                     2h-g(-z,-s)<=t<=g(z,s) }

lies in C by the lower inequality for h; its vertical intervals are
nonempty by the displayed paired-roof condition. It is centrally
symmetric about Y_h and has mixed area 2(Q-hW). Reflection therefore
proves (8) for all ambient containing halfspaces. The point Y_h belongs
to the actual fiber at z=0 because 0 lies in D and both inequalities
place h between -L and g(0,0).

In the rational example Section 5, these conditions hold throughout

    -3/8<=h<=1/4,

and the exact raw depth is 15/2-6h. In particular a negative transverse
move improves actual depth at the exact rate six until at least h=-3/8.
This improvement is proved by the paired roofs on BOTH sides, not by
section depth alone. A general body need not contain these reflected
subsets or admit one common interval of such transverse motion.

## 7. Relationship to existing obstructions and remaining scope

The archive `candidate 87728f667e65240d` already proves
exact stationary-sweep identities with an integer-tilt torque term,
refutes every universal positive-power concavity of optimized cap growth,
and gives a proper globally minimizing oblique cap whose integer-side
section tail does not transfer to the corresponding cap tail. Those are
prior results, not new claims here. Equations (3)--(4) retain the more
general two-sided projection heights and overhangs, and Sections 4--6
supply an explicit reflection certificate and an exact transverse range.

Nothing here combines the different sections of a positive circuit of
critical caps at a global deepest source. That compatibility, or another
argument using global maximality, is indispensable before the scoped
section calculations could contribute an OC proof.

## 8. Stronger contact theorem: the original section center is unique

The non-improvement in Section 3 strengthens to a strict inequality for
a proper minimizing cap. State this in general continuous dimension d>=1,
using original ambient coordinates. Let H through Y have normal (a,u),
u nonzero, and attain raw depth Q. Let its actual differentiating section
measure have total mass

    W=sum_z H_(d-1)(C_z intersect boundary H)>0,

where only original positive d-volume fibers are included. Assume the
normal derivative exists in every direction and is the ordinary signed
section integral. This holds if every cut is proper, and more generally
if every supporting trace has zero H_(d-1) measure: strict full or empty
cuts contribute zero, proper cuts contribute their usual section, and
null supporting faces have zero one-sided derivative in both directions.
For the latter statement the supporting-face graph/dominated-convergence
proof appears in
`candidate 568f7cf028ec23b6`.
At least one proper cut is an explicit sufficient condition for W>0.

Normal minimality makes the full mixed section centroid equal to Y.
For a distinct Y' in boundary(H), write Delta=Y'-Y. Perturb the normal
to (a,u)+epsilon Delta while requiring its boundary to pass through Y'.
The original cap at epsilon=0 is still H, but its derivative is

    (1/|u|) integral Delta.(X-Y') d(section measure)(X)
       =-(W/|u|)|Delta|^2<0.                            (9)

The continuous normal stays nonzero for sufficiently small epsilon.
Thus an actual halfspace through Y' has mass strictly below Q. Therefore

    depth_raw(Y')<Q for every Y'!=Y in boundary(H).       (10)

This assertion concerns every such Y' in S (and also the ambient depth
function where defined); it does not require Y' to be the centroid or a
center of the section. It forbids even an equal-depth movement within
this section. The coarea factor and ambient Euclidean norm in (9) are
those of the same coordinate system, so no nonisometric flattening is
silently used as an isometry.

A point Y' strictly inside H also has depth below Q: shift its boundary
a sufficiently small positive distance toward Y'. The shifted cap still
contains Y', and loses positive volume because at least one original
cut is proper. Consequently H meets the entire raw depth superlevel set
{D>=Q} only at Y. This is a strict contact statement for one actual
critical plane, not a global volume comparison.

The positivity W>0 must be retained. Facet-nullness and a nonzero
continuous normal do not by themselves supply a nonzero first derivative
if all traces are saturated or null supporting cuts. An own-fiber interior
source guarantees one proper own cut and hence W>0, but such interior
membership is not inferred here for every mixed global maximizer.

## 9. Conditional parity bound for actual global deepest points

**Provenance.** The no-supporting-facet parity consequence below is
already proved, through a stronger strict-interpolation theorem, in
`candidate f2d1fbdd5a877f5b`, Section 3.
The present proof records an alternative consequence of the explicit
unique-contact derivative; the parity count is not new progress.

Let Q>0 be the global raw maximum on a nonempty induced mixed set with
positive d-volume. Suppose each actual deepest point admits at least one
attaining cap satisfying the differentiability and positive-section-mass
hypotheses of Section 8. Then the set of deepest points has at most 2^n
points, with at most one point for each parity class of its integer base.
Only one qualifying cap per deepest point is required.

To prove this, suppose distinct deepest points Y1,Y2 have integer bases
of the same parity. Their midpoint Y lies in C by convexity and has an
integer base, hence Y lies in S. Halfspace depth is quasiconcave: every
closed halfspace containing Y contains at least one of Y1,Y2, and so
has mass at least Q. Thus D(Y)>=Q; global maximality gives equality.
Choose the qualifying critical cap H at this actual midpoint. It contains
at least one endpoint. Section 8 shows that any point of H other than Y
has depth strictly below Q, whether on its boundary or in its interior.
This contradicts the depth of that endpoint, proving the claim.

No arbitrary lattice transformation is used in this parity argument.
Positive-depth candidates cannot lie on original unmeasured fibers:
their integer bases lie outside conv(P), by the positive-fiber argument
in Section 1, and a strictly separating integer-coordinate halfspace
then has measured mass zero. Thus the optional positive-fiber reduction
preserves the deepest-point set as well as its depths. If its integer
affine rank is r<n, the same proof in the explicitly identified affine
lattice gives the stronger bound 2^r.

This conditional finite-center theorem is structural. It neither proves
the required regular critical cap exists at every deepest point nor gives
the OC mass fraction. In particular no argument has replaced the missing
control of multiple different critical sections by the cardinality bound.

## 10. The positive-section condition is automatic at global maximizers

There is already a complete stronger boundary exclusion in
`candidate 04819028a2421217`:
for N positive-measure fibers, actual mixed raw depth at a point in a
positive fiber is at most N times its ordinary intrinsic own-fiber depth.
Points in lower-dimensional fibers have zero depth. Consequently every
positive-depth source is in the relative interior of a top-dimensional
fiber. This applies in particular to the present full mixed-volume case
q=d. This is an existing proved result, not an assumption about the
centroid or a consequence of the new section calculation.

Therefore every nonvertical cap through a global deepest point has a
positive proper own section. The mass W>0 required in Section 8 is
automatic there. The finite-tilt theorem in
`unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)` explicitly
applies to any finite base set P in R^n with full-dimensional fibers,
not only to three fibers. Its finite-limit projection and saturation
proof supplies an attaining nonvertical cap; it also supplies continuity
on each positive fiber, so compactness and the positive own-centroid
lower bound give existence of a positive global maximum. The local
unique-contact lemma still keeps W>0 as an explicit hypothesis, since
it was stated for an arbitrary minimizing source.

It follows that Section 9's global hypothesis can be stated simply:
each global deepest point admits one attaining nonvertical cap whose
supporting traces have zero H_(d-1) measure on every positive fiber.
No additional interior or positive-section hypothesis is then needed.

### A sharp structural corollary for strictly convex fibers

This is the previously established structural corollary just identified,
with an alternative proof and an explicit count-sharpness calibration.

If d>=2 and every positive d-dimensional integer fiber is strictly
convex, the set of global deepest mixed points contains at most 2^n
points, at most one per integer parity class. Indeed each supporting
face of a strictly convex fiber is a singleton and has H_(d-1) measure
zero. Every attained nonvertical cap is therefore regular in the sense
of Section 8, while its own section is proper by the boundary exclusion.
Sections 8--9 apply. After an affine-rank reduction the bound is 2^r.
This theorem is about the NUMBER of deepest points, not their depth.

The number 2^n is attained. Take

    C=[0,1]^n times B_d,

where B_d is a centered Euclidean ball and d>=2. Each of the 2^n
integer fibers is B_d. Its centered point has raw mixed depth at least
|B_d|/2 from its own fiber alone. At each cube vertex an integer linear
functional strictly exposes that vertex among the finite base set.
A sufficiently large finite multiple of it isolates any prescribed
continuous cap of that fiber, so actual depth there is at most its own
ordinary ball depth. That ordinary depth equals |B_d|/2 only at the
ball center: a plane through any nonzero point and perpendicular to its
radial vector cuts off strictly less than half, as seen from the strictly
positive central slab. Thus the global deepest points are exactly the
2^n fiber centers. All assertions concern closed ambient halfspaces;
finite isolation uses a strict integer separation margin and bounded
continuous fibers.

For d=1 a supporting point has positive H_0 measure, so strict convexity
of an interval does not supply the null-supporting-face hypothesis.
No d=1 corollary is inferred from that phrase. Intrinsic q<d with varying
fiber direction spaces also requires a separate regularity analysis and
is outside this structural corollary.

## 11. Any centered mixed section can be realized by a minimizing proper cap

The symmetric-section hypothesis of Section 4 is unnecessary if a longer
negative extrusion is allowed. This gives an additional general
realization lemma, not merely a stationary-section construction.

Let D be a compact convex body in R^n times R^r, r>=1, and let nu be its
mixed r-dimensional measure, with total mass W>0. Suppose nu has full
affine span and its centroid Y belongs to the actual mixed section.
Translate Y to 0, using its integer base translation. Let

    R=max{|X|:X in supp(nu)},
    m0=min_(|v|=1) (1/W) integral (v.X)_+ dnu(X).

Then R>0 and m0>0. For a fixed v, a zero positive moment, together with
mean zero, would imply v.X=0 almost everywhere, contradicting the full
affine span. The moment is continuous in v by bounded convergence, so
its positive minimum on the unit sphere exists. Also m0<=R.

Choose a continuous positive concave roof g on D, let G=max_D g, and
choose

    L>=G R/m0.

For the convex body in one higher continuous dimension

    C={ (X,t):X in D, -L<=t<=g(X) },

the source (0,0) is an actual mixed point and the proper cap H={t>=0}
has EXACT raw depth

    Q=integral g dnu.                                    (11)

The original mixed (r+1)-volume is LW+Q. Thus every centered actual
mixed section can arise at a full-normal globally minimizing proper
cap; its source is not asserted to maximize depth over the whole body.

**Proof of all-direction minimality.** It is enough to consider caps
through 0. A cap with positive t coefficient can be written
{t+ell(X)>=0}, where ell is a linear functional. Its volume minus Q is
exactly

    integral clip(ell(X),-g(X),L) dnu
       >= integral clip(ell(X),-G,L) dnu.               (12)

Write ell(X)=k v.X with |v|=1,k>0; ell=0 gives equality directly.
The right side is

    integral min(k(v.X)_+,L) dnu
       -integral min(k(-v.X)_+,G) dnu.

If kR<=L, its positive term equals k integral(v.X)_+ and its negative
term is at most k integral(-v.X)_+. They agree before truncation by
mean zero, so the difference is nonnegative. If kR>L, the pointwise
bound min(kx,L)>=(L/R)x for 0<=x<=R gives a positive term at least
LWm0/R>=GW, while the negative term is at most GW. This also proves
(12)>=0.

A cap with negative t coefficient has the form {t<=ell(X)}. If ell is
nonzero, it contains the entire lower segment [-L,0] over every X with
ell(X)>=0, and therefore has mass at least

    L nu{ell>=0} >= LWm0/R >= GW >= Q.                   (13)

Here nu{v.X>0}>=Wm0/R follows from the definition of m0 and (v.X)_+<=R
on its positive set. If ell=0 the cap mass is LW>=Q directly. A cap
with zero t coefficient is a section-coordinate halfspace and obeys
the same lower bound (13). This includes pure integer normals and their
boundary mass. Every containing halfspace contains its parallel
through-source halfspace, proving the all-direction lower bound.
The flat cap attains Q, which proves (11). All positive original fibers
are cut properly because g>0 and L>0. □

This argument uses both height sides. It does not bound the normalized
source depth Q/(LW+Q) away from zero as L grows. It strengthens the
archived centroid-in-mixed-set example by proving an actual minimizing
higher-dimensional realization, something that source explicitly did
not claim.

## 12. Exact rational example: the unique section center loses original depth

Use integer bases -1,0,1 in a planar section D with continuous coordinate x:

    D={ (z,x): -1<=z<=1, 0<=x<=3-2|z| }.

The induced interval fibers are [0,1],[0,3],[0,1], their total length is
W=5, and their mixed centroid is Y=(0,11/10). Its full affine span is
R^2. Define a positive affine roof and a lower height by

    g(z,x)=31/10-x,  G=31/10, L=50.

Center the section at Y and use coordinates X=(z,s), s=x-11/10. On its
mixed support R=19/10: the central interval has endpoints s=-11/10 and
19/10, while the other endpoints have squared norm at most 221/100,
less than (19/10)^2. For a unit v=(a,b), mean zero gives

    (1/W) integral(v.X)_+ = (1/10) integral |a z+b s|.

Pairing the two outer intervals, whose common s-range is [-11/10,-1/10],
gives an absolute-moment contribution at least 2|a|. On the central
interval the subinterval [-11/10,11/10] gives at least (121/100)|b|.
Consequently

    (1/W) integral(v.X)_+
       >= (1/5)|a|+(121/1000)|b| >=121/1000.

Thus m0>=121/1000 and

    Lm0/R >=121/38 >31/10=G.

Section 11 applies to the actual three-dimensional convex body

    C={-1<=z<=1, 0<=x<=3-2|z|,
                            -50<=t<=31/10-x}.

All three integer fibers have positive area. At the actual source
(Y,0)=(0,11/10,0), the cap {t>=0} is proper on every fiber and has exact
raw depth

    Q=2 integral_0^1(31/10-x) dx
                 +integral_0^3(31/10-x) dx=10.

The total mixed area is M=260. The small normalized source depth 1/26
is not an OC counterexample: the source (0,3/2,-25) is the center of an
actual contained rectangle in its own middle fiber of area 150, so its
raw depth is at least 75 from that fiber alone.

The section's UNIQUE global deepest point is Z=(0,1), with raw section
depth two, or normalized depth 2/5. To prove the lower bound at Z, an
upward continuous cap x+alpha z>=1 captures at least two from the middle
interval. A downward cap x+alpha z<=1 captures one from the middle
interval; its two outer thresholds are 1+alpha and 1-alpha, one at least
one, so it captures a full outer interval and has total at least two.
A pure integer cap through the middle base captures length at least four.
An upward cap with alpha=0 attains two. At a middle point x<1, a sufficiently
large finite tilt of the downward cap captures exactly x plus one, less
than two; at x>1 the untilted upward cap captures 3-x<2. On either endpoint
base, a finite integer tilt isolates an ordinary interval cap of length
at most 1/2. These facts prove uniqueness of Z among the actual section
points, with all ambient directions included. At the section centroid
Y=(0,11/10), the untilted cap x>=11/10 has length 19/10<2, so its
section depth is strictly smaller.

Despite this strictly better section depth, its lift Z'=(0,1,0) has
original depth strictly less than Q. An explicit containing cap is

    t >= (x-1)/40.

Its threshold stays strictly between the lower and upper roofs on all
three fibers, because -1/40<= (x-1)/40 <=1/20<1/10<=g. Its captured area is

    10-(1/40) integral_D (x-1) dnu
       =10-(1/40)(11/2-5)=799/80<10.                   (14)

This is a finite exact witness, consistent with the unique-contact
formula. It is not only an infinitesimal or numerical claim.

Finally the vertically extended halfspace {x>=1}, which is a minimizing
section cap at Z, captures in the positive original cap exactly

    integral_1^3 (31/10-x) dx=11/5.

Relative to the positive cap Q=10 this is 11/50, strictly less than
Gamma_2/2=2/9, despite its section fraction 2/5. On the negative side its
fraction is exactly 2/5: the corresponding lower cylinder mass is 100
out of 250. Thus even the unique optimal section center and its actual
section-minimizing direction do not supply the corresponding projected
positive-cap fraction. The observation concerns the two-sided integral
transfer; it makes no claim about the depth of a measure supported only
on one cap's boundary.

## 13. The section-center loss also occurs with strict noheavy fibers

The preceding nonsymmetric example has a heavy middle fiber. The strict
loss when lifting the unique section center does not require that feature.
Use instead

    D={-1<=z<=1, 0<=x<=3/2-|z|/2},
    C=D times [-40,1].

Its section fibers are [0,1],[0,3/2],[0,1], total length W=7/2, and
mixed centroid Y=(0,17/28). Centering at Y, a support radius R<=2 suffices.
Pairing the outer intervals as in Section 12 contributes at least 2|a|
to integral|a z+b s|, and the central subinterval
[-17/28,17/28] contributes at least (289/784)|b|. Since 2W=7,

    m0 >=289/5488.

With G=1,L=40, this yields

    Lm0/R >=1445/1372>1.
